title: The Green Mountains of Asir
summary: Why the Asir mountains in southwestern Saudi Arabia are cool, rainy, and green, and how their forests, terraces, wildlife, and traditions make the region special.
poll: Mountains are better places to live than flat lands.

versions.title: Green Hills of Asir
versions.text:
Is all of Saudi Arabia hot and dry? No! Go to the southwest. You will find Asir. It is a land of tall, green mountains. The Red Sea is near.

One peak is about 3,000 meters high. It is the top of the land. Up high, the air is cool. Summer days are mild.

Wind blows in from the sea. It brings wet air. The air goes up the hills. It cools. Then it makes clouds and rain. It makes fog, too. Fog is a cloud near the ground. Asir gets lots of rain.

Tall juniper trees grow on the hills. They make dark green woods.

The hills are steep. Long ago, farmers made steps of stone. Each step is a terrace. It holds the soil. It holds the rain. Farmers grow crops like wheat and fruit there.

Big monkeys live here. They are baboons. A black and white bird lives here, too. It lives no place else.

Old homes are made of stone. Women paint the walls in bright shapes.

In summer, lots of people come here. They want to get out of the heat.

versions.title: The Green Mountains of Asir
versions.text:
When people picture Saudi Arabia, they often think of hot, sandy desert. But in the southwest, near the Red Sea, there is a land of tall, green mountains. This land is called Asir.

The mountains of Asir are the highest in the country. One peak, Jabal Sawda, rises about 3,000 meters above the sea. Air gets cooler the higher you climb. That is why summers in Asir are mild, while most other places are very hot.

Asir also gets more rain than most of the country. Winds blow in from the sea and carry wet air. When this air is pushed up the mountain sides, it cools down. The water in it forms clouds, rain, and thick fog. Fog is a cloud that sits close to the ground, and on many days it hides the mountain tops.

All this water helps juniper trees grow. These tall evergreen trees cover the hills with dark green forests.

The hills of Asir are very steep. Long ago, farmers built rows of flat steps held up by stone walls. Each step is called a terrace. It keeps the soil and the rain from washing away. On the terraces, farmers grow crops such as wheat, barley, and fruit.

Baboons live in the mountains. So does the Asir magpie, a black and white bird found nowhere else on Earth.

Many old homes in Asir are built of stone. Inside, women paint the walls with bright shapes and lines. This art is called Al-Qatt Al-Asiri.

Every summer, many families visit Abha, the main city, to enjoy the cool mountain air.

Although people who picture Saudi Arabia often imagine hot, sandy desert, in the southwestern part of the country, along the Red Sea, lies a region of tall, green mountains known as Asir.

Its tallest peak, Jabal Sawda, rises approximately 3,000 meters above sea level, and the city of Abha is located at an altitude of more than 2,000 meters. Because air becomes cooler as you climb higher, summers in Asir are pleasantly mild, while much of the country experiences extreme heat.

Asir also receives more rainfall than most of the country. Winds from the sea carry moisture, which is water vapor in the air. When this air is forced up the mountain slopes, it cools, and the water forms clouds, rain, and dense fog, which on many days wraps around the peaks like a soft blanket.

This abundant water allows juniper trees to flourish, and these tall evergreen trees cover many slopes with dark forests that provide shade and shelter for wildlife.

The slopes of Asir are extremely steep. Centuries ago, farmers constructed rows of flat steps supported by stone walls. Each step, which is called a terrace, prevents the soil and rainwater from rushing down the mountainside. On the terraces, farmers cultivate crops such as wheat, barley, and fruit.

versions.title: Asir: Where the Desert Turns Green
versions.text:
When people picture Saudi Arabia, they often imagine endless sandy desert. However, in the southwestern part of the country, along the Red Sea, lies a region of tall, green mountains known as Asir, whose landscape and climate differ remarkably from the rest of the kingdom.

The mountains of Asir are the highest in Saudi Arabia. One peak, Jabal Sawda, reaches an elevation of approximately 3,000 meters above sea level, and the city of Abha is situated more than 2,000 meters high. Because air becomes progressively cooler with increasing height, summers in Asir are pleasantly mild, while much of the country experiences extreme heat.

Asir also receives considerably more rainfall than most of the country. Winds from the sea transport moist air toward the mountains, and when this air is forced up the steep slopes, it cools until its water vapor begins to condense into tiny droplets. These droplets form clouds, rain, and dense fog that frequently envelops the peaks.

This abundant water allows juniper trees to flourish, and their forests support a rich ecosystem of plants, insects, birds, and mammals. Baboons roam the mountains, and the Asir magpie, a black and white bird found nowhere else on Earth, nests among the junipers.

Centuries ago, farmers constructed rows of flat steps supported by stone walls along the steep mountainsides. Each step, called a terrace, slows the flow of rainwater and reduces erosion, which is the gradual washing away of soil. On these terraces, farmers cultivate crops such as wheat, barley, and fruit.

Many traditional homes are built of stone, and inside, women decorate the walls with colorful geometric patterns. This art, called Al-Qatt Al-Asiri, is an essential part of the region's cultural heritage, and in 2017 UNESCO recognized it as significant to all of humanity.

Every summer, numerous families travel to Abha to escape the heat. Meanwhile, scientists and local communities are working to protect the juniper forests, because some trees are weakening as the climate becomes warmer and drier.

When people picture Saudi Arabia, they frequently imagine endless expanses of sandy desert. However, in the southwestern part of the country, along the Red Sea, lies a mountainous region known as Asir, whose landscape, climate, and culture differ remarkably from those of the rest of the kingdom.

The mountains of Asir are the highest in Saudi Arabia. One peak, Jabal Sawda, reaches an elevation of approximately 3,000 meters above sea level, and the provincial capital, Abha, is situated more than 2,000 meters high. Because the atmosphere becomes progressively cooler with increasing altitude, summers in Asir are pleasantly moderate, while much of the country endures extreme temperatures.

Asir also receives considerably more precipitation than most of the country. Prevailing winds from the sea transport humid air toward the mountains, and when this air is forced up the steep slopes, it cools until its water vapor begins to condense into microscopic droplets. These droplets generate clouds, rain, and dense fog that frequently envelops the summits for hours at a time.

This abundant moisture enables juniper trees to flourish, and their forests sustain a remarkably diverse ecosystem of plants, insects, birds, and mammals. Baboons roam the mountains, and the Asir magpie, a black and white bird found nowhere else on Earth, nests exclusively among the junipers.

Centuries ago, farmers constructed elaborate rows of flat steps supported by stone walls along the precipitous mountainsides. Each step, called a terrace, moderates the flow of rainwater and reduces erosion, which is the gradual removal of soil by water or wind. On these terraces, which have been carefully repaired by generation after generation, farmers cultivate agricultural crops such as wheat, barley, and fruit.

Many traditional homes are constructed of stone, and inside, women decorate the walls with vibrant geometric patterns. This art, called Al-Qatt Al-Asiri, represents an essential component of the region's cultural heritage, and in 2017 UNESCO officially recognized it as significant to all of humanity.

Every summer, numerous families travel to Abha to escape the heat. Meanwhile, scientists and local communities are collaborating to conserve the juniper forests, because some trees are deteriorating as the regional climate becomes increasingly warmer and drier.

versions.title: Asir: Where the Desert Turns Green
versions.text:
When people picture Saudi Arabia, they frequently imagine endless expanses of sandy desert. Nevertheless, in the southwestern part of the country, along the Red Sea, lies a mountainous region known as Asir, whose landscape, climate, and culture differ remarkably from those of the rest of the kingdom.

The mountains of Asir are the highest in Saudi Arabia. One peak, Jabal Sawda, reaches an elevation of approximately 3,000 meters above sea level, and the provincial capital, Abha, is situated more than 2,000 meters high. Because the atmosphere becomes progressively cooler with increasing altitude, summers in Asir are pleasantly moderate, while much of the surrounding country endures exceptionally severe temperatures.

Asir also receives considerably more precipitation than most of the country. Prevailing winds from the sea transport humid air toward the mountains, and when this air is forced up the steep slopes, it cools until its water vapor begins to condense into microscopic droplets, which generate the clouds, rain, and dense fog that frequently envelop the summits for hours at a time.

This abundant moisture enables juniper trees to flourish, and their forests sustain a remarkably diverse ecosystem of plants, insects, birds, and mammals. Baboons roam the mountains, while the Asir magpie, a black and white bird found nowhere else on Earth, nests exclusively among the junipers, making the survival of these forests particularly significant.

Centuries ago, farmers constructed elaborate rows of flat steps supported by stone walls along the precipitous mountainsides. Each step, called a terrace, moderates the flow of rainwater and reduces erosion, which is the gradual removal of soil by water or wind, and on these terraces, which successive generations have carefully maintained, farmers cultivate agricultural crops such as wheat, barley, and fruit.

Many traditional homes are constructed of stone, and inside, women decorate the walls with vibrant geometric patterns. This art, called Al-Qatt Al-Asiri, represents an essential component of the region's cultural heritage, and in 2017 UNESCO officially recognized it as an element of intangible heritage significant to all of humanity.

Every summer, numerous families travel to Abha to escape the intense heat of the lowlands. Meanwhile, scientists and local communities are collaborating to conserve the juniper forests, because some trees are deteriorating as the regional climate becomes increasingly warmer and drier. The disappearance of these forests would endanger the entire mountain ecosystem.

questions.stem: What did UNESCO do in 2017?
options: It named Jabal Sawda the highest peak in Arabia.
It began protecting the Asir magpie.
It built new terraces in Abha.
It recognized Al-Qatt Al-Asiri.
questions.why: The article states that in 2017 UNESCO recognized Al-Qatt Al-Asiri as significant to all of humanity.

wrong.A: The article does not link UNESCO to Jabal Sawda.
wrong.B: The article does not say UNESCO protects the magpie.

questions.stem: Why would losing the juniper forests be especially serious for the Asir magpie?
options: The magpie feeds only on rainwater.
The magpie nests among the junipers and lives nowhere else.
The magpie needs fog to fly.
The magpie migrates to the Red Sea in summer.
questions.why: Since the bird nests among junipers and exists nowhere else, losing the forests could threaten the whole species.

wrong.A: The article does not say what the magpie eats or drinks.
wrong.C: Nothing in the article connects fog and flight.
wrong.D: The article does not mention magpie migration.

questions.stem: What can you infer about the farmers who first built the terraces?
options: They understood how water moves on steep land.
They did not need to grow any food.
They lived near flat desert plains.
They built them only for decoration.
questions.why: Building steps that slow rainwater and reduce erosion shows they understood how water and soil behave on slopes.

wrong.B: Terraces were built to grow crops such as wheat and barley.
wrong.C: They lived on steep mountainsides, not flat plains.
wrong.D: The terraces had a practical purpose: farming and protecting soil.

questions.stem: "Its water vapor begins to condense into tiny droplets." What does condense mean here?
options: To disappear completely into the sky
To heat up quickly
To change from a gas into liquid drops
To freeze into hard, solid ice crystals
questions.why: Water vapor is a gas; when it condenses, it turns into tiny liquid droplets that form clouds and fog.

wrong.A: The water does not disappear; it forms clouds, rain, and fog.
wrong.B: The air cools rather than heats.
wrong.D: The article describes droplets, not ice.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article with information about protecting the juniper forests?
options: To show that the forests are no longer important
To blame summer visitors for every problem
To explain how to plant and water a juniper tree at home
To show a challenge that people are working to solve
questions.why: After describing what makes Asir special, the author points out a threat and the efforts to protect it.

wrong.A: The author shows the forests matter a great deal.
wrong.B: The article does not blame visitors.

questions.stem: How does Asir's climate compare with much of the rest of Saudi Arabia?
options: It is hotter and drier.
It is cooler and rainier.
It is the same, but windier.
It is colder only at night.
questions.why: The article says summers in Asir are mild and that it receives more rain than most of the country.

wrong.C: The article stresses differences in temperature and rainfall.
wrong.D: The article says summers are mild, not just nights.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how Asir's elevation affects its climate, plants, and people. Use evidence from the article to show how these ideas are connected.
checklist: I explained at least two effects of elevation.
I used specific evidence from the article.
I showed how the causes and effects are connected.
